Memo to "Diamond" Subscribers:
For many years The Diamond of Psi Upsilon was issued in November, January,
March and June. In order to conform more nearly with the current picture and postal
regulations, we have a FaU Convention issue. Winter undergraduate issue, covering Fall
activities, Spring undergraduate issue with the first notice of the Convention program,
and a Summer issue essentiaUv about alumni activities and carrying a second notice of
the coming Convention.
The Convention used to be held in June, interfering with graduation activities, closing
of the Chapter Houses, June house parties, visiting with relatives, and preparations for
leaving college. Now, with more pleasant weather and much less confusion by holding
the Convention in September, there is really no reason for a
Chapter letter until some time
later when the Associate Editors in the Chapters have some interesting news to send to
The Diamond.

By Laurance G. Wolfe, Rho '48

THE 59-yeai--old photograph gracing the
cover of The Diamond is of Sterling
Goodale Hadley, Theta 1836, one of Psi
Upsilon's Founders. The photo was made
available through the courtesy of the man
who took it. Brother John E. Becker, Psi
'03.
Brother Becker conducts the Becker-Mc
Lean fire insurance agency in Waterloo,
New York, with John E. Becker, Psi '35.
The agency was
originally owned by
Brother Hadley, who sold it to the Mc
Lean Brothers in 1894. It became part of
the Becker-McLean Company in 1910.
Brother John E. Becker reports that he
snapped the picture of the illustrious
Brother Hadley in 1900 on the latter's
front porch. Brother Becker still uses the
fine old walnut desk which was
presented
to Brother Hadley by Willard State Hos
pital when Hadley was
president of that
institution.
With the photograph which was loaned
to The Diamond at the request of Brother
WiUiam Falconner, Jr., Delta Delta '49,
came the following thumb-nail sketch of
Brother Hadley's career written by Brother
John E. Becker.
"Sterling Goodale Hadley, Theta, 1836,
was the first president of Psi Upsilon. He
was
graduated from Union College and
was a member of Phi Beta Kappa. Soon
after his graduation he began the study
of law at Avon Springs, N.Y., under
George Hosmer, in 1836-1837, and then
under Hon. Samuel Birdsall, at Waterloo,
N.Y., in 1837-1839. He was admitted to
the bar in 1839 and practiced law at
Waterloo until his retirement in Septem
ber, 1897.
"Brother Hadley held many responsible
positions in the community. For years he
was the President of Willard State Hos
pital, one of the great institutions of Seneca
County, which in 1892 named Hadley
Hall, its then new theatre and meeting
place, in honor of him. He was a Member
of Assembly from the county in 1853 and
Seneca County Judge and Surrogate for
the years 1856 to 1860. He was a
very
competent attorney and active in all com
munity affairs. He was
Village of Water
loo Clerk in 1839; village attorney in 1847,
1850 and 1854; President of the village
for part of a
year, and a school trustee for
the years 1847 to 1853 and 1858 to 1860.
He presided at the organization meeting
of The First National Bank of Waterloo
and was a director of that bank from 1864
to 1882; Register in Bankruptcy for sev
eral counties from 1865 to 1883; Presi
dent of the Waterloo Library and Histori
cal Society from 1877 to 1881, and a
Trustee of Hobart College for a number
of years. Brother Hadley owned the first
typewriting machine in the Seneca County
area.
"Brother Hadley was one of the older
substantial men of Seneca County. He was
highly regarded and respected by all of
the learned residents of the community in
which he lived."

By Eugene Vinet,
[Eugene Vinet, Epsilon Phi '11, recently pre
sented the Psi Upsilon headquarters office
�with an owl sculptured from soapstone. He
also arranged for a mould to be made from
the original work and a
replica of the soapstore owl to be cast in bronze for presenta
tion to the Epsilon Phi chapter. At the re

has written this account of his artistic en
deavor.]
In visits to various chapter houses of Psi
Upsilon over a
period of years, I had noticed
that Psi U's beloved owl was not on
display
in some houses, and in many was a
decrepitlooking stuffed bird who did not do justice to
the fratemity or the chapter. Mounted owls
in various shapes, sizes, and colors bore mute
testimony to a lack of interest in the physical
representation of our "ancient owl."
But it wasn't until 1958 that I thought I
might be able to do something about design
ing an owl worthy of Psi U's great tradi
tions.
I had completed fairly successful training
in landscape painting and charcoal portraiture
in retirement in Florida. Suddenly I thought
that painting and drawing might be an excel
lent springboard to an
attempt at sculpture.
With the encouragement of a few Psi U
brothers in whom I confided my ambition, I
set to work to try my hand at becoming a
sculptor. I wanted to design a
permanent owl
for good old Psi Upsilon!
Brother Ed Peattie, editor of The Diamond,
obtained for me a book on how to carve
animals�especially birds and fish�written by
Brother John L. Lacey, Delta Delta '25.
The face of the screech owl with its
"horns" appealed to me the most, but it is
quite a small bird, too small for what I had
in mind and I didn't like the way the claws
showed up. It became evident that as a sym
bolic figure my work would have to be a com
posite of several owls.
In looking over books on
sculpture I saw
that beginners sometimes use
soap blocks.
While visiting my sister in Montreal during
the summer months I obtained a
piece of
castile soap about six inches high. After mak
ing a few sketches to study the type of base
and how the bird should stand I proceeded
with a small potato peeling knife found in a
kitchen drawer. The result was not only my

CaUow accepted, but on one conditionthat his post would be temporary. It was

fused several times, even

fered the largest salary in rowing history�

rowing coach. He was getting $6,600

While he was
wrestling with the offer, he
was
besieged by Washington adherents�fac
ulty, alumni and undergraduates�to remain

It was at Penn that he reaUy came into

It was at Penn that he became known as a
man with a
dry barbed wit that made him
one of the most sought-after dinner speakers
in athletics. And at Navy he has become an
object of veneration and affection that few
men achieve.
He had been at Penn for 23 years when
he decided to go to Navy. Why? Simply be
cause he detested the Penn rowing course on
the silty Schuylkill River. It has since been
de-silted, but at that time he didn't believe

"The SchuylkiU," he said then, "is the only

is a
dirty business. It's much too thick to
drink and much too thin to plow."
He moved on to Navy at no increase in
salary. "I don't want any more
money. I
don't need it," he explained. He just wanted
a
spot where he could have a fair chance of
producing top crews. He did, too.
But he refused to claim any personal credit
for his crews. Asked, once, what makes a
great
crew, he answered: "Well, it certainly isn't the

One of his crews, in a five-boat regatta on
Lake Onondaga a few years back, turned in
a record for the two-mile course. Callow re
fused to believe the watches. "The course
must be short," he said. "Let's check it."
He was assured the course had been care
fully surveyed.
"Then we must have been rowing downhiU," he muttered.
One evening, before a recent I.R.A. regatta
here. Navy's three crews were about to shove
off for their workout. A cameraman from a
local newspaper which had helped underwrite
the regatta asked Callow to line up the crews
so that he could catch them under the bridge.
Callow was a little skeptical.
"What paper you from?" he asked.
He was told.
"Well, in that case," replied the Sage of
the Severn, "we'll even row over the bridge."
One evening, at one of these same Stewards
Dinners that honored CaUow last night, Cal
low was a featured speaker. The Sage twitted
his coaching confrere, Al Ulbrickson, now re
tired at Washington but known, in his hey
day, as the Dour Dane.
"You know," said Callow, I don't think it's
quite right that the Washington crew should
have an objective that we don't have. I un
derstand that ever since Washington finished
seventh in the I.R.A. last year there's been a
slogan posted all over the waUs of the Wash
ington boathouse. 'Sink the Navy,' it reads.
"Well, I thought we
ought to have an objec
tive, too. Of course at Navy the objective al
ways is 'Beat Army'. But Army has no crew.
I thought we'd have to pick somebody else.
But who?
"So I put the name of every possible op
ponent into a hat and decided to pick one out
and make that one the tea;m we had to beat.
"I picked Rutgers.
"What happened?
"Rutgers didn't send a crew to the regatta
that year."
It may be unsentimental, even unkind, to
speculate on such a thing as retirement, volun
tary or
unvoluntary, for our
boy. But when
and if it does happen. Young Man Callow
will have contiibuted more to the amateur sport
of rowing, and amateur it truly is, than any
man in the game today.
That's why they honored Rusty CaUow last
night.
